title: After an expected home death: the first call and the right to pause

source_packet.source_basis: Public-source practice-layer synthesis for schema testing; no private testimony, no contributor interview, no claim of corpus completeness.
limitations: Public sources describe recognized care patterns but do not supply firsthand room texture.
This record must not become procedure-level instruction for a particular death.
Treatment, legal, ritual, emergency, and equipment decisions remain local and must be handled by qualified teams or relevant authorities.

moment.plain_scene: The person has died at home after an expected dying process. The room is quiet, nobody is sure how quickly to call, and witnesses need to know that the first call belongs to the care plan and local rules, not panic alone.
ordinary_language_queries: what do I do when someone dies at home
who do I call when hospice patient dies
can I sit with the body after death
do I need to call ambulance after expected death
how long can we wait after death at home

content_layers.observation_text: Public after-death sources describe calling the relevant doctor, palliative or hospice team, or planned contact after an expected home death; some also note that immediate emergency response may not be required when the death is expected and a plan exists.
content_layers.source_synthesis: Marie Curie, Macmillan, and healthdirect support the basic scene while demonstrating jurisdictional variation. The record must not become universal legal instruction.

interpretation.editor_interpretation: This record protects the pause. The first minutes after death are not only administration; they are also the last shared room, bounded by local rules and care arrangements.

what_this_is_not: not a universal instruction about ambulance, police, doctor, coroner, or funeral home
not a reason to delay required reporting
not a replacement for the person’s care plan or local authority guidance
uncertainties: Rules differ by country, state, setting, expected/unexpected death, and care plan.
Sudden, suspicious, violent, custody, pediatric, or unexplained deaths are outside this low-risk record.
Family wishes, religious practice, and professional availability may change the sequence.
content_layers.lay_orientation: A lay surface should say: use the plan and local care contacts; an expected home death may allow a pause, but the required first call depends on place and circumstances.
content_layers.practitioner_notes: A practitioner surface should collect pre-death preparation scripts: who to call, what not to do automatically, how to preserve dignity, and how to make room for ritual.
language_notes: Use “expected home death” rather than generic “death at home.”
Avoid “you do not have to call…” without jurisdiction.

provenance.provenance_statement: Drafted from named public sources to test the practice layer. It should be reviewed before any public surface uses it.

safety.clinical_boundary: This record is observational/source-indexing only. It is not medical advice, not a prognosis, not a legal instruction, not a ritual authority, and not a substitute for a local hospice, clinician, emergency, legal, cultural, or care team.
safety.safety_notes: Before public use, route through clinical or domain review and ensure any lay surface directs urgent, worried, legal, medication, swallowing, equipment, or body-handling questions to qualified local support.
